newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan weekly uses photo of boy arrested in murder.
newsitem.headline: Japan weekly uses photo of boy arrested in murder.

text.p: The arrest of a self-confessed 14-year-old suspect in a grisly murder that has shocked Japan took another twist on Wednesday when a photo magazine broke a taboo and carried his photograph.

The use of the photograph in the weekly Focus magazine, which hit newsstands on Wednesday, came after anonymous contributors to some web sites on the Internet revealed what appeared to be the name of the suspect.
Police have kept the suspect's identity under wraps because the strict Juvenile Law says authorities must not reveal names and details of criminal suspects under 18 years of age.
Most Japanese media have kept to this rule, although the law does not specify that the media should do so.

As word of the photograph in Focus spread through the distribution network, many convenience store chains, railway and subway kiosks as well as bookstores voluntarily removed copies from their shelves, store officials said.
The magazine's action brought harsh criticism from government leaders.
"The police and most mass media are making every effort to protect the privacy of the family and the suspect himself," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said.
"I don't see what benefit this would bring," Hashimoto told reporters. "The publisher should not break long-held rules just because it made its own decision."
Officials of the Justice Ministry's Civil Liberties Bureau said they would question the publishers of the magazine for possibly violating the boy's human rights.
The suspect was arrested last Saturday after police said he confessed to the murder of his childhood playmate, 11-year-old Jun Hase.

On May 27, Jun's severed head was found at the foot of the front gate of a junior high school in Kobe with a note stuck in the mouth saying the murderer, who called himself the "School Killer", was taking revenge against the education system.
The arrested boy was a pupil at the school.
Shinchosha Ltd, the publisher of Focus, said it printed the arrested boy's photograph because the case was an exceptional one.

"We judged that the case went beyond the framework of the Juvenile Law because of its extremely idiosyncratic nature which shocked the entire nation," Igo Yamamoto, deputy chief editor of Focus, said in a statement.
"Although we expected criticism, we decided to deal with it the same way as ordinary (murder) cases and publish the photograph," Yamamoto said.
